paragraphs.text: Christ goes of his own accord into a garden, which his betrayer knew, to be taken, so that by his obedience he might take away the sin that entered into the world by one man's rebellion, and that in a garden.
Christ who was innocent was taken as a wicked person, that we who are wicked might be let go as innocent.
Christ's person (but not his power) was bound by his adversaries, but only when and how he desired.
Christ does not neglect the office of a good pastor, not even in his greatest danger.
We ought to contain our zeal for God within the bounds of our calling.

paragraphs.text: Christ is brought before an earthly high priest to be condemned for our blasphemies, that we might be acquitted by the everlasting high Priest himself.
paragraphs.anchor: And led him away to Annas

paragraphs.text: A graphic example of the fragility of men, even the best of them, when they are left to themselves.
Christ defends his cause, but only slightly, not that he would withdraw himself from death, but to show that he was condemned as someone who was innocent.
paragraphs.anchor: The high priest then asked Jesus

paragraphs.text: After men have once fallen, they cannot only not lift themselves up by their own strength, but also they fall more and more into a worse condition, until they are raised up again by a new power from God.
paragraphs.anchor: And Simon Peter stood and warmed

paragraphs.text: The Son of God is brought before the judgment seat of an earthly and profane man, in whom there is found much less wickedness than in the rulers of the people of God. A graphic image of the wrath of God against sin, and in addition of his great mercy, and last of all of his most severe judgment against the stubborn condemners of his grace when it is offered unto them.
